desc:
You stand on the top-left cell of the m x n matrix grid and want to reach the bottom-right cell, moving one step up, down, left or right at a time. The score of a path is the smallest value among all cells it visits, including the first and the last cell.

Return the largest score any path from the top-left to the bottom-right cell can achieve.

grid = [[5, 4, 5],
        [1, 2, 6],
        [7, 4, 6]]
path 5 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> 6 has score 4
no path avoids both the 4 and the 1/2 cells, so result = 4
hints: Instead of searching for the best path directly, ask a yes/no question: for a given threshold t, can you reach the goal using only cells with value ≥ t?

If a path exists using only cells ≥ t, the same path works for every smaller threshold, so the answer to the yes/no question is monotone in t. The best score is one of the values that appear in the grid.
Sort the distinct values (or binary search over [0, 10^9]) and for each probe t run a BFS/DFS from the top-left cell over cells ≥ t. Find the largest t whose search reaches the bottom-right cell.
editorial: Define reach(t) as 'the bottom-right cell is reachable from the top-left one using only cells with value ≥ t' (it is false right away if either end cell is below t). If a path works for t it works for every t' < t, so reach is true for small thresholds and false for large ones. The answer is the largest t with reach(t) = true; it always equals some cell value, namely the smallest cell on an optimal path.

Binary search over the sorted distinct cell values: each probe is one flood fill (BFS) in O(m n), and there are O(log(m n)) probes. The largest feasible value is the answer; the smaller of the two end cells always works, so a feasible value exists.

Total time is O(m n log(m n)) (the sort plus the probes) and the space is O(m n). A priority queue that always expands the largest unvisited frontier cell (a Dijkstra variant) reaches the same result, and so does a union-find that adds cells from the largest value downwards until the two end cells join.
